**LOS ANGELES (CNN)** — Maurice Jarre, the Academy Award-winning composer behind the iconic scores of cinematic classics such as *Doctor Zhivago* and *Lawrence of Arabia*, passed away from cancer in Los Angeles on Sunday. He was 84 years old.

Jarre enjoyed a distinguished career collaborating with legendary Hollywood directors, including John Huston, Alfred Hitchcock, and, most prominently, David Lean. Speaking to CNN on Monday, fellow French composer Alexandre Desplat—who interviewed Jarre for *The Screening Room* at the Berlin International Film Festival last month—remarked, "Maurice was an immense artist, an incredible symphonist, a magician of melody, and a benevolent human being."

Jarre claimed Academy Awards in 1963 and 1966 for his acclaimed scores for Lean’s *Lawrence of Arabia* and *Doctor Zhivago*, respectively. He went on to earn six additional Oscar nominations, securing his third Academy Award in 1984 through yet another fruitful partnership with Lean on *A Passage to India*. Later in his career, Jarre transitioned from traditional orchestral composition to become a pioneer in electronic scoring, crafting memorable soundtracks for films such as *Witness*, *Fatal Attraction*, *Dead Poets Society*, and *Ghost*.

Around the same time, his son, Jean-Michel Jarre, established himself as one of the world’s foremost electronic music artists, renowned for global hits such as "Oxygène" and grand outdoor concert spectacles. The senior Jarre’s final film composition was for the 2000 feature *I Dreamed of Africa*.

Although his versatile body of work encompassed symphonies, ballets, and theater, it was his 150 film scores that earned him an honorary Golden Bear at the Berlin International Film Festival last month—nearly half a century after producer Sam Spiegel first hired him for *Lawrence of Arabia*. Festival director Dieter Kosslick commended him in a statement late last year, noting, "Film composers often exist in the shadows of great directors and acting stars. It is different with Maurice Jarre; the music of *Doctor Zhivago*, like so much of his work, is world-famous and remains unforgotten in the history of cinema."

During his interview in Berlin with Desplat—a two-time Oscar nominee himself for *The Queen* and *The Curious Case of Benjamin Button*—Jarre reflected on his creative partnerships: "I never really had a 'bust-up' with a good director. A good director will always find an intellectual understanding. And that's what was great—I had an opportunity with all these people. I don't think I can say that I ever worked with a bad director." 

However, Jarre also observed that directing legends of the caliber of Huston and Hitchcock had disappeared, adding, "The only problem is now, there is more and more bad music that goes 'dang dang dang dang dang...' So... it's better to turn off the music, and listen to a concert of Mozart."

*Senior producer Neil Curry and associate producer Lidz-Ama Appiah contributed to this report.*

**Symphonies of the Silver Screen: The Enduring Legacy of Maurice Jarre**

When acclaimed composer Maurice Jarre passed away at the age of 84, the world of cinema lost one of its most transformative sonic architects. Over a career that spanned more than half a century, the French-born composer redefined how music interacts with moving images. By crafting the musical backdrops for over 150 films, Jarre proved that a score is not merely background sound, but a vital, living character capable of driving narrative and evoking deep emotional landscapes. 

Jarre’s rise to international prominence is inextricably linked with his legendary partnership with director David Lean. In 1962, Lean hired a relatively unknown Jarre to score the epic *Lawrence of Arabia*. Given just six weeks to compose nearly two hours of music, Jarre delivered a masterpiece. His sweeping, percussion-heavy main theme captured both the terrifying grandeur and the haunting solitude of the desert, earning him his first Academy Award. The Lean-Jarre collaboration would become one of the most celebrated in cinema history, yielding two more Oscar wins for the tragic romance of *Doctor Zhivago* (1965)—whose "Lara’s Theme" became a global pop culture phenomenon—and the atmospheric *A Passage to India* (1984).

While Jarre was revered for his lush, classical orchestral arrangements, he was never trapped by tradition. He possessed a restless, pioneering musical spirit that pushed him to explore uncharted sonic territories. Long before electronic music became a staple of Hollywood filmmaking, Jarre was experimenting with unique instrumentation, including the early electronic instrument known as the Ondes Martenot. By the 1980s, he fully embraced modern technology, seamlessly blending traditional symphonic elements with electronic synthesizers and global ethnic instruments. 

This daring fusion was showcased in a diverse array of classic films. For Peter Weir’s *Witness* (1985), Jarre famously scored a drama set in Amish country almost entirely with synthesizers, creating a hypnotic and surprisingly organic texture that earned him yet another Oscar nomination. His groundbreaking electronic and hybrid scores for films like *Fatal Attraction* (1987), *Dead Poets Society* (1989), and *Mad Max Beyond Thunderdome* (1985) demonstrated an extraordinary versatility that kept him at the forefront of the industry across radically different genres.

Jarre’s monumental contributions were recognized worldwide. Beyond his three Academy Awards out of nine nominations, he was honored with a Lifetime Achievement Award at the 2009 Berlin International Film Festival, where he received an Honorary Golden Bear shortly before his death. His artistic lineage also carried into the future through his son, Jean-Michel Jarre, who himself became a global icon in electronic music.

Historically, film scoring was often viewed as a secondary craft, designed to sit quietly in the shadows of Hollywood's towering directors and charismatic movie stars. Maurice Jarre changed that paradigm forever. Through his extraordinary melodic sense, bold experimentation, and grand cinematic vision, he elevated film music to a primary art form. Though the maestro has passed, his grand desert themes, sweeping waltzes, and innovative synthscapes remain immortalized on celluloid, continuing to inspire filmmakers and music lovers around the globe.

"Maurice was a giant of film music, a master of melody who understood how to give a film its soul," said fellow Oscar-winning composer Hans Zimmer. "His work on *Lawrence of Arabia* wasn't just a score; it was a character in the film. Every composer working today owes a debt to his vision."

French electronic music pioneer Jean-Michel Jarre, the composer’s son, released a brief statement honoring his father’s legacy: "My father was a pioneer who lived entirely for his passion. He taught me that music is a universal language that transcends borders and generations. His sound will live on forever."

Film composer John Williams also paid tribute, praising Jarre’s unique melodic gift. "Maurice possessed a rare talent for capturing the grandeur of human emotion on a vast canvas. 'Lara’s Theme' and the magnificent overture to *Lawrence of Arabia* are immortal touchstones of our art form. He was a gracious colleague and a true artist."

Born in Lyon, France, in 1924, Jarre originally studied engineering before committing himself to music at the Conservatoire de Paris, where he studied percussion and composition. He spent years writing music for French theater and short films before making his leap to Hollywood in the early 1960s.

In 1994, Jarre was awarded a star on the Hollywood Walk of Fame, and in 2009—just weeks before his death—he was honored with a Lifetime Achievement Award at the Berlin International Film Festival.

Jarre is survived by his wife, Fong F. Khong; his sons, Jean-Michel and Kevin; and his daughter, Stéfanie.

# Legendary Oscar-winning composer Maurice Jarre dies at 84

**By Nischelle Turner, CNN Entertainment Correspondent**  
*Updated 10:45 AM EDT, Monday, March 30, 2009*

**LOS ANGELES (CNN)** — Maurice Jarre, the French-born master composer whose soaring, lush, and emotionally resonant film scores gave epic scale to cinema classics like *Lawrence of Arabia* and *Doctor Zhivago*, has died in Los Angeles. He was 84.

Jarre passed away peacefully in his sleep on Sunday night following a battle with cancer, according to his manager, Fabienne Gassmann. 

Over a career that spanned more than half a century, Jarre wrote the music for over 150 motion pictures, working alongside legendary directors such as David Lean, John Huston, Luchino Visconti, and Peter Weir. He was nominated for nine Academy Awards, winning three—all for his celebrated collaborations with Lean.

---

---

### The Sound of the Epic

It was Jarre’s work with director David Lean that elevated him into the pantheon of Hollywood legends. In 1962, Lean tapped the relatively unknown French composer to score *Lawrence of Arabia*. Jarre famously had just six weeks to write two hours of orchestral music. 

The result was a masterpiece: a dramatic, sweeping theme that mirrored the vastness of the Arabian desert, utilizing exotic percussion alongside a traditional Western orchestra. The score earned Jarre his first Oscar and instantly redefined the sound of cinematic epics.

Three years later, Jarre teamed with Lean again for *Doctor Zhivago* (1965). The soundtrack produced "Lara’s Theme," a haunting, balalaika-driven melody that became an international pop phenomenon. The soundtrack album sold millions of copies worldwide, topped the Billboard charts, and earned Jarre his second Academy Award.

---

> *Composer Maurice Jarre backstage at the 57th Academy Awards in 1985 after winning the Oscar for Best Original Score for David Lean's "A Passage to India." (Photo: Michael Ochs Archives/Getty Images)*

---

His third Oscar came for Lean's 1984 drama *A Passage to India*, cementing one of the most successful director-composer partnerships in film history.

"Maurice had an extraordinary ability to capture the landscape of a film in a single melody," film historian Leonard Maltin told CNN. "Whether it was the sands of the Sahara, the snows of Russia, or the heat of India, he didn't just write background music—he painted the emotional backdrop of the entire story."

### Embracing Innovation

While best known for his massive symphonic arrangements, Jarre was never one to be trapped by tradition. In the 1980s, he surprised Hollywood by embracing electronic synthesizers, proving that a classical composer could reinvent himself for a modern era.

His electronic score for Peter Weir’s 1985 thriller *Witness*, starring Harrison Ford, earned him another Oscar nomination. The film’s famous "building the barn" sequence—scored entirely with layered, rhythmic synthesizers—remains a masterclass in film editing and music integration.

Jarre went on to compose memorable scores for a strikingly diverse array of films, including *Fatal Attraction* (1987), *Gorillas in the Mist* (1988), *Dead Poets Society* (1989), and the blockbuster romantic fantasy *Ghost* (1990).

---

### A Musical Dynasty

Born in Lyon, France, in 1924, Jarre initially studied engineering at the Sorbonne before defying his father's wishes to pursue music at the prestigious Paris Conservatoire. He started his career as a percussionist before becoming the musical director of the Théâtre National Populaire in Paris, where he honed his skills writing stage music.

Music ran deep in the Jarre bloodline. His son, Jean-Michel Jarre, became a global superstar and pioneer in electronic ambient music, famous for his record-breaking laser-and-synthesizer stadium concerts. 

"My father was a giant," Jean-Michel Jarre said in a statement released through his publicist on Monday. "His music touched generations, and his passion for sound will live on forever."

Tributes poured in from across the entertainment world on Monday. 

Former French President Nicolas Sarkozy hailed Jarre as a "great French composer" who possessed "a generous and majestic vision of cinema." 

The Academy of Motion Picture Arts and Sciences released a statement calling Jarre "a visionary artist whose scores helped define the golden age of widescreen storytelling."

Maurice Jarre is survived by his wife, Fong F. Khong; his sons, Jean-Michel and Kevin; his daughter, Stéfanie; and several grandchildren. 

Private funeral services are expected to be held in Los Angeles later this week, with a public memorial event in Paris to be announced at a later date.
